```{r, include = FALSE}
knitr::opts_chunk$set(collapse = TRUE, comment = "#>", message = TRUE, warning = TRUE)
```

A predicted mean is a linear combination of the model's coefficients. When some
treatment combinations have no data, or two factors are confounded, some of these
combinations cannot be estimated from the data: emmeans prints them as `nonEst` and SAS
as `Non-est`. This vignette shows what predictmeans does in these cases and how to get
means and comparisons that are estimable.

In short:

- **Cell means** of combinations with no data are not shown.
- **A mean that averages over an empty cell** (e.g. the mean of a nitrogen level over
  the varieties when one variety lacks that level) keeps the rule of predictmeans 1.x:
  it is the average of the observed cells, with a warning naming it.
- **Its comparisons** with other means are made on the cells both means have (column
  `over` of `pairs`), not as the difference of two averages over different cells.
- **The table says so**: column `over` of `means` names the cells such a mean averages.
  Nothing read off the means can contradict the pair tests: when its pairs are not
  the differences of the shown means, such a mean has no comparison interval,
  `letterCI` takes the letters from the p-values, and `autoplot()` draws no
  comparison or half-LSD bar for it (an open point marks every such mean).
- **A cell** is a combination of the factors of one interaction term of the model.
  Factors that do not interact do not make cells together: a combination of them
  without data is not an empty cell, because an additive model can estimate it.
- **Confounded factors** (two factors that do not interact in the model and do not
  occur in all combinations, so that their effects cannot be told apart): the mean over
  all their combinations does not exist. The means average over the combinations that
  exist, with a warning that names the two factors and says how to state the structure
  in the model.
- **Means that still cannot be estimated** are `NA`, with a message. Their pairwise
  differences are given when they can be estimated, and letters among those.
- The `means` table has an `estimable` column and the number of observations, `n`.

```{r, message = FALSE, warning = FALSE}
library(predictmeans)
```

## An empty cell

Suppose the plots of Victory at the highest nitrogen level were lost in the oats split
plot:

```{r}
Oats <- as.data.frame(nlme::Oats)
Oats$N <- factor(Oats$nitro)
Om <- subset(Oats, !(Variety == "Victory" & N == "0.6"))
with(Om, table(Variety, N))
fm <- lmer(yield ~ N * Variety + (1 | Block/Variety), data = Om)
```

The model with the interaction has one coefficient fewer (lme4 drops it). The cell means
are those of the 11 combinations with data:

```{r, warning = FALSE}
pm_cells <- predictmeans(fm, "N:Variety", plot = FALSE)
nrow(pm_cells$means)
```

The nitrogen means average over the varieties. For N = 0.6 only two varieties have data,
so its mean is their average, and predictmeans warns:

```{r}
pm_n <- predictmeans(fm, "N", plot = FALSE)
pm_n$means[, c("N", "over", "estimate", "std.error", "n")]
```

That mean leaves out Victory, the lowest-yielding variety at the other nitrogen levels,
so it is too high compared with the others; emmeans calls it non-estimable. The
difference 125.8 − 79.4 = 46.4 would mix the nitrogen effect with the variety effect
(Victory is in the mean of N = 0 but not in that of 0.6). So predictmeans compares N = 0.6
with each other level on the varieties both have, Golden Rain and Marvellous (column
`over`): 0.6 − 0 is the average of their two differences, 42.5. Pairs among the complete
levels are the differences of the means as usual:

```{r}
pm_n2 <- suppressWarnings(predictmeans(fm, "N", pairwise = TRUE, plot = FALSE))
pm_n2$pairs[, c("level1", "level2", "over", "estimate", "std.error", "p.value")]
```

Comparing the two averages instead would wrongly call 0.6 and 0.4 different here (p = 0.03
against 0.08 on the common varieties). In simulations (`dev/review-defaults.md` in the
package sources) comparing averages over different cells rejected 8–78% of true null
hypotheses when the other factor had an effect; comparing on the common cells 4–6%. When
two means have no cell in common their difference is NA (`over = "none"`). `pm_joint()`
tests a term on the cells common to all its means, and `contrastmeans()` compares on the
cells the means of each contrast have in common. `anova()` does the same for its Type III
tests: the interaction keeps the contrasts that use no empty cell (5 df here, not 6), and
the main effects are the `pm_joint()` tests:

```{r}
anova(fm)
```

The mean of N = 0.6 stays in the table, labelled by `over`, because it is the honest
estimate of its own quantity (the average over the varieties that have it). A table of
means over the cells common to all levels would not be better: it would change the means
of complete levels whenever another level loses a cell, and with scattered empty cells
the cells common to all can shrink to one or none. Readings that treat the means as
comparable are switched off for it instead: no comparison interval (its pairs are on
common cells), letters from the p-values with `letterCI = TRUE`, an open point in
`autoplot()`:

```{r, fig.width = 5, fig.height = 3.5}
ggplot2::autoplot(pm_n2, interval = "comparison")
```

Other comparisons that stay within the observed cells are sound too, e.g. nitrogen levels
within each variety:

```{r, warning = FALSE}
pm_v <- predictmeans(fm, "N:Variety", atvar = "Variety", adj = "tukey", plot = FALSE)
within <- subset(pm_v$pairs, !is.na(by))
head(within[, c("level1", "level2", "by", "estimate", "p.adj")])
```

or contrasts written with `specify_contrast()`, which refuses means that cannot be
estimated:

```{r, warning = FALSE}
cm <- specify_contrast(Kmatrix(fm, "N:Variety"),
  N_effect_GR_and_M = (`0.6:Golden Rain` + `0.6:Marvellous`)/2 - (`0:Golden Rain` + `0:Marvellous`)/2)
contrastmeans(fm, "N:Variety", ctrmatrix = cm)[[1]]
```

## What counts as a cell

A cell is a combination of the factors of one interaction term. In
`y ~ date/farm + date*trt` the cells are date × farm and date × treatment; farm and
treatment do not interact. Suppose treatment B has no data on farm F2 at date d2:

```{r}
set.seed(11)
dft <- expand.grid(rep = 1:3, trt = factor(c("A", "B")), farm = factor(c("F1", "F2")),
                   date = factor(c("d1", "d2")))
dft <- dft[!(dft$date == "d2" & dft$farm == "F2" & dft$trt == "B"), ]
dft$y <- 5 + as.integer(dft$farm) * as.integer(dft$date) + 0.5 * (dft$trt == "B") +
  rnorm(nrow(dft), 0, 0.3)
fd <- lm(y ~ date/farm + date*trt, data = dft)
predictmeans(fd, "date:trt", plot = FALSE)$means[, c("date", "trt", "estimate", "n")]
```

Every date × farm and every date × treatment cell has data, and the model says the
treatment effect is the same on both farms, so the mean of B at d2 over both farms can be
estimated: no empty cell, no warning. (An average over farm F1 only would make B look
worse than A just because F1 is the poorer farm.) With a farm × treatment interaction in
the model (`date/farm*trt`) the same combination is an empty cell, and the rule of the
first section applies.

## Confounded factors

In this spray trial the highest spray volume was used only with fine droplets, and the
other two volumes only with medium droplets:

```{r}
set.seed(3)
spray <- data.frame(
  droplet = factor(rep(c("medium", "fine"), c(40, 10)), levels = c("medium", "fine")),
  vol = factor(c(rep(c("130", "200"), 20), rep("400", 10))),
  conc = factor(rep(c("none", "half"), 25)))
spray$y <- 5 + 0.3 * (spray$conc == "half") - 0.4 * (spray$droplet == "fine") +
  rnorm(50, sd = 0.2)
with(spray, table(droplet, vol))
```

In a model with `droplet` and `vol` as separate factors, the effect of volume 400 cannot
be told apart from that of fine droplets. A volume mean averaged over both droplet sizes
needs both, so it cannot be estimated. `predictmeans()` then averages over the
droplet–volume combinations that exist and says so:

```{r, warning = TRUE}
fs <- lm(y ~ droplet + conc + vol, data = spray)
pv <- predictmeans(fs, "vol", pairwise = TRUE, plot = FALSE)
pv$means[, c("vol", "estimate", "std.error", "n", "group")]
```

Read these means with the warning in mind: "volume 400" is "volume 400 with fine
droplets", and its difference from volume 130 is also a difference between droplet sizes.
The data cannot separate the two.

### Three ways to say what you want

The warning names three ways to get the means without relying on the fallback. They are
not the same mean:

| Way | What the mean is |
|---|---|
| Write the nesting in the formula (`droplet/vol`) | equal-weight average over the combinations that exist; the same numbers as the fallback, without the warning about confounding |
| Leave out the factor that adds nothing (when one factor is determined by the other, as a farm by its pastures) | equal-weight average over the levels that remain; the same numbers again |
| `weights = "cells"` | average over the observed combinations weighted by their numbers of observations; depends on how the data are spread over the other factors |

The first two change the formula, not the fit: the fitted values and the likelihood are
the same. Stating the structure in the model is the better record of the design:

```{r}
fs2 <- lm(y ~ conc + droplet/vol, data = spray)
pn <- predictmeans(fs2, "vol", plot = FALSE)
cbind(pn$means[, c("vol", "estimate")], fallback = pv$means$estimate,
      cells = predictmeans(fs, "vol", weights = "cells", plot = FALSE)$means$estimate)
```

### Confounded within another factor

Confounding is not always nesting over the whole data set. In a grazing trial sampled on
several dates, each pasture type is on one farm at a date, but a pasture type can be on
another farm at a later date:

```{r, warning = TRUE}
set.seed(5)
past <- rbind(expand.grid(date = c("d1", "d2"), pasture = c("P1", "P2", "P3", "P4"),
                          trt = c("A", "B"), rep = 1:3),
              expand.grid(date = "d3", pasture = c("P1", "P4"), trt = c("A", "B"), rep = 1:3))
past$farm <- ifelse(past$date == "d3", ifelse(past$pasture == "P1", "F3", "F4"),
                    ifelse(past$pasture == "P4", "F2", "F1"))
for (v in c("date", "pasture", "trt", "farm")) past[[v]] <- factor(past[[v]])
past$y <- as.integer(past$date) + as.integer(past$pasture)/2 + 0.5*(past$trt == "B") +
  rnorm(nrow(past), 0, 0.3)
fp <- lm(y ~ date/farm + date/(trt + pasture)^2, data = past)
pp <- predictmeans(fp, "date:trt", plot = FALSE)
```

Farm and pasture do not interact in the model, and at each date the farm is known from
the pasture: the farm terms add nothing to the fit (their coefficients are aliased). The
package finds the pair of factors by trying: it leaves out the combinations without data
of one pair at a time (first pairs among the factors averaged over) and keeps the first
choice with which every mean can be estimated. The means equal those of the model
without `farm`:

```{r}
fp0 <- lm(y ~ date/(trt + pasture)^2, data = past)
p0 <- suppressWarnings(predictmeans(fp0, "date:trt", plot = FALSE))
cbind(pp$means[, c("date", "trt", "estimate")], without_farm = p0$means$estimate)
```

(The remaining warning for `fp0` is about date d3, where two pasture types were not
sampled: an ordinary empty cell.)

Before this rule (decided 2026-11-16) such means were `NA`; in predictmeans 1.x they were
the same averages, without a warning that said why.

## Checklist

- Look at the `n` and `estimable` columns of the `means` table, and at warnings and
  messages.
- Compare means that average over the same cells; use `atvar` or contrasts within the
  observed cells when some are empty.
- When the warning says two factors are confounded, the means are over the combinations
  that exist. Write the structure into the model (nesting, or leave out the factor that
  adds nothing) so that the model says what the means are; `weights = "cells"` gives a
  different, frequency-weighted mean.
